doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Count Basie band and Thad Jones
title: Writing to the Basie band and learning its book
summary: He wanted to play in the big bands, wrote to Basie members through the booking office, and had the Basie charts memorized from playing along with records.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: You mentioned an anecdote about getting to see Count Basie and so forth. Did you have aspirations to play in the big bands that were still around as a young man?

Yeah absolutely. And I started a relationship with some of the guys in the band too because they’d come about three or four times a year to Minnesota, where I was living at the time. And I’d say look what’s your address? And they gave me the address of Willard Alexander, the booking in New York that booked every big band I later found out — you know 660 Madison Avenue, New York, NY 1002 — whatever it was. It was the address, and you could just write, “The guy in the band, Count Basie Orchestra, Willard Alexander, 660 Madison Avenue,” and I never forgot that address, because I would write this bass trombone player, Bill Hughes, the manager, or trumpet player at the time, Sonny Cohn, and I’d see these guys and I’d ask them questions and this and that, and so they sort of knew me from that. And I went with a bunch of bands before the Basie band, but then when they finally heard about me, they were like, “That’s that kid that used to write us letters.” And one thing that’s important to that band is that you know the music. You know if you go in the drum chair in the Count Basie band, most of the charts are missing to the standards like “Shiny Stockings,” and “One O’Clock Jump,” and “Whirley-Bird,” and all the hits. There’s no music to those. And really there shouldn’t be and doesn’t have to be because if you’re going in that band you have to know the music enough to play it by memory as the drummer. And even me when I went I had the shout chorus to “Shiny Stockings” memorized because I just had played it with records so many times. “One © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

O’Clock Jump” I had because I played that with records. You know you stand in a room and you pretend like you’re lead trumpet player and you play with the records, like we’ve all done. And that’s something that everybody has to do at some period in their lives. So yeah I definitely had aspirations to do it, and I’d already done it anyway in drill at home in my basement.
